Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google's AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or  …

title: Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
summary: Classic video games are being decompiled and recompiled to run on new hardware and platforms, including web browsers and VR headsets, though these projects operate in legal gray areas and often involve AI assistance. Examples include Halo in web browsers, Zelda ports to non-Nintendo hardware, and unofficial remakes with enhanced features.
content:
It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever imagined skateboarding in Call of Duty? Or playing the original Halo right in your web browser, complete with multiplayer?  
These are unofficial versions of games, so they may sit in a legal gray area. It seems unlikely that Nintendo, for example, is particularly happy about people finding ways to play The Legend of Zelda on non-Nintendo hardware. Many of these projects are also made with the assistance of AI, which, for some people, is a non-starter given ethical or environmental concerns surrounding the technology.
Below, you’ll find our coverage of gaming decomps, recomps, and all the other ways gamers are reverse-engineering games to go previously unimaginable places.
Here’s a video of Half-Life: Alyx running natively on a Vision Pro.
			
Just think: You could be playing Halo in a web browser right now.
			
This unofficial Lego Racers remake runs in your browser with split-screen and online multiplayer.

title: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
summary: The Matic robot vacuum became the first robovac added to the FCC's ban waiver list, though ironically it doesn't need the waiver since its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC's foreign drone and robot bans only affect future products, not existing ones.
content:
The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it's also now the first to escape the FCC's Roomba ban. 
Well, sort of - because the Matic wasn't banned to begin with. 
Here's what's actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale. 
But the Matic doesn't need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC's foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing o …

title: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
summary: AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic have announced major breakthroughs on mathematical problems, including a Millennium Prize Problem solution, but their rapid progress has sparked academic backlash over concerns about proper attribution and methodology. The industry faces mounting pressure to prove it's learning from earlier missteps.
content:
This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.

TCL’s P80 Ultra is its first Nxtpaper phone with an OLED screen. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge

title: Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI
summary: The article argues that human cognition is far more complex than the computer-based analogies used by AI industry leaders like Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk suggest. Industry figures often reduce human intelligence to biological computations, overlooking the deeper complexity of actual human thinking. Fundamental misunderstandings about human intelligence could lead to flawed AI development approaches and unrealistic expectations about AI capabilities.
content:
Norbert Wiener, godfather of cybernetics, once said, "The thought of every age is reflected in its technique." For the past century, our thought has been reflected in our computers, including by those in the AI industry. Google's Demis Hassabis calls the brain "a biological approximation to a Turing machine." Elon Musk puts it more bluntly, declaring that "people should just think of the brain as a biological computer." (Musk's brain often worries me.)
But humans are more complex than a straightforward comparison to computers gives us credit for - and far more than most of the AI industry seems to appreciate. And as their products push e …

content: Fresh analysis of First Dynasty mass burials finds signs of fatal blunt force trauma on 39 percent of skulls
